entries.title: II Samuel 13:1
segments: Great beauty, great honor, high station, and much property, are often the occasion of ruin to the possessor.  They should therefore not be coveted.  If bestowed, they should be employed to the honor of God and the good of men; and if not bestowed, we should be contented without them.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:2
segments:
Thought it hard; difficult or impracticable. 
 
Were the power of men equal to their wickedness, virtue would be constantly outraged, and earth become an emblem of hell.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:3
segments: Wicked men in high stations are ordinarily surrounded by subtle flatters, who labor to secure their favor by tempting them to the commission of sin, and thus become the means of their destruction.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:5
segments:
Make; feign, pretend to be. 
 
  Dress the meat; cook him some food, pretending that she could do it better than any one else.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:6
segments: No deception is so gross, and no wickedness so horrible, that licentious men in high stations will not practise it with cool deliberation and determined purpose.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:12
segments: Natural affection, gratitude, and all kindly feelings, the dictates of conscience, regard to consequences, and every thing which stands in the way of sinful gratification, will be disregarded by those who surrender themselves to its power.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:19
segments: There are injuries inflicted which in this world can never be repaired, and distresses which none but God can assuage.  Though he permits such injuries, he does not forget them, nor does he fail in due time to visit their authors with his wrath.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:21
segments:
Was very wroth; but took no measures to inflict punishment upon Amnon for his crime.  This leniency seems to have proceeded partly from parental fondness, and partly from the recollection of his own heinous crime. 
 
It is not enough for rulers to be angry at the foul crimes of their subjects; they should punish them, that others may fear and be restrained from practising such iniquities.  Nor, while they remember with shame their own sins, and the injurious influence they may have exerted on others, should they let natural affection or a sense of their own guilt hinder them from doing their duty.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:24
segments: Sheep-shearers; at sheep-shearing it was customary to make a feast and invite friends.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:28
segments: When rulers, whose office it is to punish crime, neglect their duty, the natural result is the commission of further crimes.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:29
segments: One wicked man, in the indulgence of his hateful passions, may be the instrument of executing not only his own wrath, but the just indignation of God against another, and then in due time be himself punished, and that for ever and ever.

entries.title: II Samuel 13:39
segments: Comforted concerning Amnon; was less grieved at his death, than at the absence of Absalom.
